goal.title: Reason about food-web energy and measurement
goal.learningTarget: Reason about food-web energy and measurement
contentTopics: Production versus standing biomass and transfer efficiency
goal.focusAreas: Production versus standing biomass and transfer efficiency

sourceDocuments.name: Synthetic study notes
sourceDocuments.text: In this simplified annual food web, energy production is measured in kJ per year, and standing biomass in g at one instant. Transfer efficiency from a prey to a consumer is consumer production attributable to that prey divided by prey production, with both over the same interval. Diet shares describe fractions of consumer intake, not fractions of prey production eaten. Standing biomass alone does not determine annual production.

text: {"questions":[{"prompt":"In a simplified annual food web, phytoplankton have standing biomass 500 g and annual production 2000 kJ. Zooplankton consume only phytoplankton, have standing biomass 200 g, and annual production 400 kJ. A fish species consumes 50% zooplankton and 50% phytoplankton by diet share, has standing biomass 100 g, and annual production 100 kJ. What is the transfer efficiency from zooplankton to fish?","explanation":"Transfer efficiency is consumer production attributable to a specific prey divided by that prey's production. The fish's total production is 100 kJ. Since diet share describes fractions of consumer intake (not prey production eaten), and assuming intake proportions reflect production attribution, 50% of fish production (50 kJ) is attributable to zooplankton. Zooplankton production is 400 kJ. Transfer efficiency = 50/400 = 12.5%. Standing biomass figures are irrelevant to this calculation.","expectedAnswer":"12.5%","choices":["12.5%","25%","50%","20%"],"topic":"Production versus standing biomass and transfer efficiency","skillID":"production-standing-biomass-transfer-efficiency","objectiveID":"calculate-transfer-efficiency-with-diet-shares","objective":"Calculate transfer efficiency using diet shares and distinguish from standing biomass ratios","difficulty":4,"format":"Multiple Choice"},{"prompt":"A marine food web study reports: kelp standing biomass 8000 g with annual production 4000 kJ; sea urchin standing biomass 600 g with annual production 600 kJ; sea otter standing biomass 40 g consuming only sea urchins with annual production 40 kJ. A researcher claims the kelp-to-urchin transfer efficiency exceeds the urchin-to-otter efficiency, proving energy pyramids can invert. What error invalidates this conclusion?","explanation":"The researcher compared standing biomass ratios (600/8000 = 7.5% for kelp-to-urchin, 40/600 = 6.7% for urchin-to-otter) rather than transfer efficiencies. Actual transfer efficiencies are production-based: urchin production/kelp production = 600/4000 = 15%, and otter production/urchin production = 40/600 = 6.7%. The kelp-to-urchin efficiency (15%) actually exceeds the urchin-to-otter efficiency (6.7%), but this is normal trophic transfer, not an inverted pyramid. The error is using standing biomass instead of production for efficiency calculations.","expectedAnswer":"Standing biomass was used instead of production to calculate transfer efficiencies","choices":["Standing biomass was used instead of production to calculate transfer efficiencies","The diet share assumption was violated by exclusive consumption","Annual intervals cannot measure transfer efficiency in this system","The trophic level assignment of kelp is incorrect"],"topic":"Production versus standing biomass and transfer efficiency","skillID":"production-standing-biomass-transfer-efficiency","objectiveID":"identify-standing-biomass-production-confusion","objective":"Identify when standing biomass is incorrectly substituted for production in efficiency calculations","difficulty":4,"format":"Multiple Choice"}]}

text: {"questions":[{"prompt":"In a lake food web, phytoplankton have standing biomass 50 g and annual production 10,000 kJ. Zooplankton have standing biomass 20 g and annual production 2,000 kJ, consuming only phytoplankton. A fish species has standing biomass 100 g and annual production 500 kJ, with diet 80% zooplankton and 20% benthic invertebrates (production 2,500 kJ). What is the transfer efficiency from zooplankton to fish?","explanation":"Transfer efficiency equals consumer production attributable to a prey divided by prey production. Fish production from zooplankton is 80% of 500 kJ = 400 kJ. Zooplankton production is 2,000 kJ. Efficiency = 400/2,000 = 20%. Standing biomass values are irrelevant to this calculation.","expectedAnswer":"20%","choices":["2%","4%","20%","50%"],"topic":"Production versus standing biomass and transfer efficiency","skillID":"production-standing-biomass-transfer-efficiency","objectiveID":"calculate-transfer-efficiency","objective":"Calculate transfer efficiency using production values, not standing biomass","difficulty":4,"format":"Multiple Choice"},{"prompt":"A grassland has grass with standing biomass 2,000 kg and annual production 50,000 kJ. Grasshoppers have standing biomass 50 kg. If grasshopper production is 5,000 kJ and they consume only grass, but a bird species with standing biomass 10 kg gets 60% of its energy from grasshoppers and 40% from grass seeds (which constitute 10% of total grass production), what constrains the bird's maximum possible annual production?","explanation":"Bird production from grasshoppers is limited by grasshopper production available to birds. Grasshopper production is 5,000 kJ; birds could access at most this amount from that source. From grass seeds, birds could access at most 10% of 50,000 kJ = 5,000 kJ. The grasshopper pathway constrains production because even with 100% transfer efficiency, only 5,000 kJ is available from grasshoppers versus 5,000 kJ from seeds. Standing biomass figures (2,000 kg grass, 50 kg grasshoppers, 10 kg birds) do not determine these production limits.","expectedAnswer":"Grasshopper production limits the bird's production from that energy pathway","choices":["Grass standing biomass limits bird production","Grasshopper standing biomass limits bird production","Grasshopper production limits the bird's production from that energy pathway","Bird standing biomass limits total ecosystem production"],"topic":"Production versus standing biomass and transfer efficiency","skillID":"production-standing-biomass-transfer-efficiency","objectiveID":"distinguish-production-biomass-constraints","objective":"Distinguish whether production or standing biomass constrains energy transfer","difficulty":4,"format":"Multiple Choice"}]}

text: {"questions":[{"prompt":"In a simplified annual food web, phytoplankton have standing biomass 500 g and annual production 2000 kJ. Zooplankton consume only phytoplankton, have standing biomass 200 g, and annual production 400 kJ. A fish species consumes zooplankton (60% of diet) and also phytoplankton directly (40% of diet). The fish has standing biomass 100 g. If fish production attributable to zooplankton equals 60% of zooplankton production consumed by fish, and fish production attributable to phytoplankton equals 40% of phytoplankton production consumed by fish, what is the fish's annual production?","explanation":"First, find zooplankton-to-fish transfer efficiency: fish gets 60% of zooplankton production it consumes as its own production, so 0.60 × (zooplankton production consumed). sourceDocuments.name: Synthetic study notes
sourceDocuments.text: In this simplified annual food web, energy production is measured in kJ per year, and standing biomass in g at one instant. Transfer efficiency from a prey to a consumer is consumer production attributable to that prey divided by prey production, with both over the same interval. Diet shares describe fractions of consumer intake, not fractions of prey production eaten. Standing biomass alone does not determine annual production.

input.difficultyGuidance: Connect multiple reasoning steps or resolve interacting constraints.

questions.prompt: In a simplified annual food web, phytoplankton have standing biomass 500 g and annual production 2000 kJ. Zooplankton consume only phytoplankton, have standing biomass 200 g, and annual production 400 kJ. A fish species consumes 50% zooplankton and 50% phytoplankton by diet share, has standing biomass 100 g, and annual production 100 kJ. What is the transfer efficiency from zooplankton to fish?
questions.explanation: Transfer efficiency is consumer production attributable to a specific prey divided by that prey's production. The fish's total production is 100 kJ. Since diet share describes fractions of consumer intake (not prey production eaten), and assuming intake proportions reflect production attribution, 50% of fish production (50 kJ) is attributable to zooplankton. Zooplankton production is 400 kJ. Transfer efficiency = 50/400 = 12.5%. Standing biomass figures are irrelevant to this calculation.
questions.topic: Production versus standing biomass and transfer efficiency
questions.objective: Calculate transfer efficiency using diet shares and distinguish from standing biomass ratios

questions.prompt: A marine food web study reports: kelp standing biomass 8000 g with annual production 4000 kJ; sea urchin standing biomass 600 g with annual production 600 kJ; sea otter standing biomass 40 g consuming only sea urchins with annual production 40 kJ. A researcher claims the kelp-to-urchin transfer efficiency exceeds the urchin-to-otter efficiency, proving energy pyramids can invert. What error invalidates this conclusion?
questions.explanation: The researcher compared standing biomass ratios (600/8000 = 7.5% for kelp-to-urchin, 40/600 = 6.7% for urchin-to-otter) rather than transfer efficiencies. Actual transfer efficiencies are production-based: urchin production/kelp production = 600/4000 = 15%, and otter production/urchin production = 40/600 = 6.7%. The kelp-to-urchin efficiency (15%) actually exceeds the urchin-to-otter efficiency (6.7%), but this is normal trophic transfer, not an inverted pyramid. The error is using standing biomass instead of production for efficiency calculations.
questions.expectedAnswer: Standing biomass was used instead of production to calculate transfer efficiencies
choices: Standing biomass was used instead of production to calculate transfer efficiencies
The diet share assumption was violated by exclusive consumption
Annual intervals cannot measure transfer efficiency in this system
The trophic level assignment of kelp is incorrect

questions.objective: Identify when standing biomass is incorrectly substituted for production in efficiency calculations

questions.prompt: In a lake food web, phytoplankton have standing biomass 50 g and annual production 10,000 kJ. Zooplankton have standing biomass 20 g and annual production 2,000 kJ, consuming only phytoplankton. A fish species has standing biomass 100 g and annual production 500 kJ, with diet 80% zooplankton and 20% benthic invertebrates (production 2,500 kJ). What is the transfer efficiency from zooplankton to fish?
questions.explanation: Transfer efficiency equals consumer production attributable to a prey divided by prey production. Fish production from zooplankton is 80% of 500 kJ = 400 kJ. Zooplankton production is 2,000 kJ. Efficiency = 400/2,000 = 20%. Standing biomass values are irrelevant to this calculation.

questions.objective: Calculate transfer efficiency using production values, not standing biomass

questions.prompt: A grassland has grass with standing biomass 2,000 kg and annual production 50,000 kJ. Grasshoppers have standing biomass 50 kg. If grasshopper production is 5,000 kJ and they consume only grass, but a bird species with standing biomass 10 kg gets 60% of its energy from grasshoppers and 40% from grass seeds (which constitute 10% of total grass production), what constrains the bird's maximum possible annual production?
questions.explanation: Bird production from grasshoppers is limited by grasshopper production available to birds. Grasshopper production is 5,000 kJ; birds could access at most this amount from that source. From grass seeds, birds could access at most 10% of 50,000 kJ = 5,000 kJ. The grasshopper pathway constrains production because even with 100% transfer efficiency, only 5,000 kJ is available from grasshoppers versus 5,000 kJ from seeds. Standing biomass figures (2,000 kg grass, 50 kg grasshoppers, 10 kg birds) do not determine these production limits.
questions.expectedAnswer: Grasshopper production limits the bird's production from that energy pathway
choices: Grass standing biomass limits bird production
Grasshopper standing biomass limits bird production
Grasshopper production limits the bird's production from that energy pathway
Bird standing biomass limits total ecosystem production

questions.objective: Distinguish whether production or standing biomass constrains energy transfer

questions.prompt: In a simplified annual food web, phytoplankton have standing biomass 500 g and annual production 2000 kJ. Zooplankton consume only phytoplankton, have standing biomass 200 g, and annual production 400 kJ. A fish species consumes zooplankton (60% of diet) and also phytoplankton directly (40% of diet). The fish has standing biomass 100 g. If fish production attributable to zooplankton equals 60% of zooplankton production consumed by fish, and fish production attributable to phytoplankton equals 40% of phytoplankton production consumed by fish, what is the fish's annual production?
questions.explanation: First, find zooplankton-to-fish transfer efficiency: fish gets 60% of zooplankton production it consumes as its own production, so 0.60 × (zooplankton production consumed). But fish production attributable to zooplankton is also defined as 60% of total fish production. Let F = total fish production. Then 0.60F = 0.60 × (zooplankton consumed), so zooplankton consumed = F. Similarly, 0.40F = 0.40 × (phytoplankton consumed), so phytoplankton consumed = F. Total consumption by fish = 2F. Energy balance: fish production = consumption × assimilation efficiency. From the definitions, production attributable to each prey equals diet share fraction × total production, and also equals (transfer efficiency fraction) × (prey production consumed). Solving: 0.60F = 0.60 × C_z, so C_z = F; 0.40F = 0.40 × C_p, so C_p = F. The production-to-consumption ratio for fish is F/(2F) = 0.50. Checking: 0.60F from zooplankton requires consuming F worth of zooplankton production at 60% efficiency; 0.40F from phytoplankton requires consuming F worth of phytoplankton production at 40% efficiency. Total fish production is 200 kJ.

questions.prompt: An annual food web contains plants with standing biomass 800 g and annual production 1600 kJ. Herbivores have standing biomass 400 g. A predator has standing biomass 150 g, annual production 90 kJ, and consumes only herbivores with a transfer efficiency of 15% from herbivore production to predator production. If herbivore standing biomass alone cannot determine their annual production, which additional single piece of information would allow calculating herbivore annual production?
questions.explanation: Predator production = 0.15 × (herbivore production consumed by predator). Since predator consumes only herbivores, herbivore production consumed = predator production / 0.15 = 90/0.15 = 600 kJ. However, this is only the portion eaten, not total herbivore production. To find total herbivore production, we need to know what fraction of herbivore production is consumed by this predator (or equivalently, the herbivore's total production or its consumption rate by all predators). The herbivore's production-to-biomass ratio, consumption rate by all predators, or fraction of herbivore production eaten by this predator would suffice. Among standard ecological measures, knowing the herbivore's annual production-to-biomass ratio (P/B) allows calculation: production = P/B ratio × standing biomass.
choices: The herbivore's assimilation efficiency
The herbivore's production-to-biomass ratio
The predator's assimilation efficiency
The plant's transfer efficiency to herbivores
